A realization from 4 months of job searching:

Every interview I've had has come through a person.

Not a perfectly optimized resume. Not a cover letter. Not an AI prompt.
A person.

Job applications today can feel like a race. Hundreds of applicants, countless resumes, and an increasing amount of content generated by AI. Recruiters are sorting through an overwhelming volume of candidates, while applicants are doing everything they can to stand out. I've been fortunate enough to make it to several final rounds during my search, and every one of those opportunities started with a conversation, a referral, or someone willing to take a few minutes to help.

That's not to say resumes don't matter. They do. But this experience has reminded me that relationships still matter more.

So if you're hiring, keep reaching out to people you trust.

And if you're searching, don't spend all your time clicking "Apply." Spend some of it talking to people.

It's made all the difference for me.

Stanford + Meta has recently dropped a paper that flips everything about AI agents.

It's called "Code as Agent Harness."

Right now, we treat large language models as text generators. When they need to solve a complex problem, they rely on a "chain of thought."

But natural language is slippery. It's vague. It loses context. When an agent hallucinates in English, it just keeps talking.

So they introduced a framework that changes the entire architecture of autonomy: "Code as Agent Harness."

They stopped asking the AI to reason in words, and forced it to reason in code.

Code isn't just the final output anymore. It is the memory. It is the environment. It is the boundary.

Instead of writing a paragraph about how to solve a problem, the agent writes a script, executes it, and reads the output.

Tests become its senses. Execution logs become its memory. Sandboxes become its physics.

If an agent makes a mistake in English, it apologizes and hallucinates again.

If an agent makes a mistake in code, the compiler throws an error. The trace tells it exactly what broke. The system forces it to fix it.

This is where prompt engineering dies, and systems engineering takes over.

The paper proves that reliability doesn't come from a smarter base model. It comes from the "harness" wrapped around it:

- The model proposes.

- The harness executes.

- The environment returns feedback.

- The verifier checks

New Career Paths in the AI Era ☕

AI is not only changing the tools we use.

It is also changing the career paths available to us.

In today’s Coffee with AI, I presented some of the new — and not-so-new — career paths emerging in the world of Artificial Intelligence.

Some of these roles have existed for a long time. But with the rise of LLMs, AI has quickly become one of the most important topics for anyone working in, or thinking about working in, technology.

For people already in tech, this is a great opportunity to build on existing skills and start a new professional cycle — or simply become more productive and effective in their current role.

*A backend developer can become an AI Engineer.
*A project manager can start building AI-powered applications.
*A DevOps engineer can expand into MLOps.

But building AI solutions is no longer exclusive to technical professionals.

One great example is Mike Brown, a personal injury lawyer who participated in the Built with Opus 4.6 Claude Code hackathon.

His project, CrossBeam, uses AI to help address California’s housing permitting bottleneck by analyzing blueprints, correction letters, and permit-related documents to generate a clear action plan for approval.

That is remarkable.

Not long ago, coding hackathons were spaces almost exclusively reserved for programmers. Today, AI is making it possible for domain experts — lawyers, doctors, musicians, infrastructure specialists, project managers, and many others — to turn their expertise into working solutions.

Most companies are still figuring out how to use AI as a competitive advantage. And the speed of change in this field is incredible.

That is why we created Coffee with AI here at Plan A: to help our team stay aligned, curious, and inspired by the many possibilities Artificial Intelligence is opening up.

🚀 Just spent the weekend diving into agentic AI frameworks — #AutoGPT, #n8n, #HuggingFace Agents, and #Hermes Agent—and I keep coming back to how refreshingly straightforward Hermes Agent feels while still packing serious power.  What sets Hermes Agent apart for me is its skill‑first architecture. Instead of wrestling with endless YAML or wrestling with complex prompt chains, you extend Hermes by adding or writing skills (think: reusable, shareable capabilities) with a simple hermes skill install or hermes skill create. Want to read email, run terminal commands, or talk to a local LLM? There’s likely a skill for it, and if not, building one is straightforward Python. Compare that to the boilerplate‑heavy setup of AutoGPT or the task‑loop‑centric design of BabyAGI, and you’ll see why I can go from idea to a working agent in minutes, not hours.  That said, each framework shines in its own way:  - AutoGPT excels at autonomous, goal‑driven looping with minimal human‑in‑the‑loop tuning.  - BabyAGI is fantastic for exploring task‑generation loops and memory‑centric architectures.  - Hermes Agent gives you a balanced, extensible platform where you can mix‑and‑match skills, configure APIs via hermes config set, and still drop down to custom code when you need it.  If you’re experimenting with agentic AI and want a platform that lets you start small, grow complexity gradually, and share your building blocks with the community, Hermes Agent is worth a spin.  🔧 Curious: Which agentic AI framework have you experimented with, and what feature matters most to you when choosing one?
